lesson.title: Mapping Numbers: The Number Line
lesson.summary: The number line turns the abstract idea of order and distance into a visual, physical picture, using absolute value to measure how far any number sits from zero or from another number.
lesson.body:
The number line is a geometric picture of the real numbers: a straight line where every point corresponds to exactly one real number, and every real number corresponds to exactly one point. A fixed point is chosen to represent zero, positive numbers extend to the right, and negative numbers extend to the left, spaced out using a consistent unit distance. This turns an abstract idea, comparing and ordering numbers, into something visual and physical: you can literally see that 5 is farther right than 2, and that -3 is to the left of -1.

The number line makes ordering numbers intuitive: for any two numbers, the one farther to the right is greater. This immediately clarifies a common trouble spot with negative integers. Even though 7 is greater than 3 in magnitude, -3 is greater than -7, because -3 sits to the right of -7 on the line, closer to zero. Distance from zero, regardless of direction, is called absolute value, written with vertical bars; |-7| = 7 and |3| = 3, since both are 7 and 3 units from zero respectively.

Absolute value has a clean formal meaning: |a| = a when a is zero or positive, and |a| = -a when a is negative, which makes the result positive, since the negative of a negative number is positive. For example, |-9| = -(-9) = 9. Absolute value is used constantly to measure distance between two points on the number line: the distance between numbers a and b is |a - b|. The distance between -4 and 3 is |-4 - 3| = |-7| = 7, which matches counting the 7 unit steps between them visually.

Worked example: order the numbers -2, 5, -8, 0, and 3 from least to greatest, and find the distance between the least and greatest. Placing them mentally on the number line from left to right gives -8, -2, 0, 3, 5, so that is the order from least to greatest. The least value is -8 and the greatest is 5. The distance between them is |5 - (-8)| = |5 + 8| = |13| = 13 units, which also matches simply counting the span from -8 to 5 directly on the line.

The number line also gives geometric meaning to inequalities. The statement x > 2 describes every point to the right of 2, while x <= -1 describes every point at or to the left of -1, including -1 itself. Graphing these regions as shaded rays on the number line, with an open circle at 2 for a strict inequality and a closed circle at -1 for a non-strict one, turns an abstract inequality into a picture you can read directly. This visual habit carries forward directly into graphing inequalities in two variables on the coordinate plane.

The number line builds on both Number and Integers, since it needs the full sweep of positive and negative values, evenly spaced, to serve as reliable landmarks. It is also the direct ancestor of the coordinate system covered next: by taking one number line and crossing it with a second number line at a right angle, you gain the ability to locate points in two dimensions rather than just one. Every skill practiced here, ordering, absolute value, distance, carries over unchanged when you start plotting points in the plane.
